name: Comparing Classical and Operant Conditioning
what: Classical and operant conditioning are both behaviourist three-phase approaches to learning, but they differ in the type of behaviour learned (involuntary versus voluntary), the role of the learner (passive versus active), and the mechanism of learning (stimulus association versus consequence).
why: Comparison questions appear regularly in VCAA exams and require students to articulate both similarities and differences with precision; confusing the mechanisms of each approach is a common source of lost marks.

items.title: I can identify the key similarities between classical conditioning and operant conditioning
items.what: Both classical and operant conditioning are behaviourist approaches to learning, both involve three sequential phases, and both require repeated trials for learning to occur. Neither approach attributes learning to internal thought processes; both focus on observable behaviour shaped by the external environment.
items.why: Questions that ask for similarities are just as common as those asking for differences, and students who only memorise differences will be unable to answer these correctly.
items.example: In both Pavlov's dog experiment and a dog being trained to sit with treats, multiple repeated pairings or consequences were needed before the dog reliably displayed the learned behaviour.

items.title: I can explain the key difference between the type of behaviour learned in each approach
items.what: Classical conditioning results in an involuntary learned response: the learner has no conscious control over the conditioned response. Operant conditioning results in a voluntary learned behaviour: the learner consciously acts and the consequence shapes whether they act that way again.
items.why: The involuntary/voluntary distinction is the most fundamental difference between the two approaches and is tested in both multiple-choice and short-answer questions.
items.example: Samia sweating when she tries on a new apron at a store is involuntary (classical conditioning). Bethany choosing to study to avoid taking out the bins is voluntary (operant conditioning).

items.title: I can explain the difference in the role of the learner across the two approaches
items.what: The learner is passive during classical conditioning: they do not consciously choose to produce the conditioned response. The learner is active during operant conditioning: they voluntarily produce a behaviour that is then shaped by its consequence.
items.why: Passive versus active is a direct point of comparison assessed in the study design and in VCAA exam questions asking students to compare the two approaches.
items.example: In Little Albert's case, the infant did not choose to fear the white rat; the fear response was passively conditioned. In contrast, a student who starts studying more because they receive good marks for effort is actively altering their behaviour based on a consequence.

items.title: I can link the type of behaviour in each conditioning approach to the division of the nervous system involved
items.what: Classical conditioning typically involves the autonomic nervous system, which controls involuntary responses of visceral muscles, organs, and glands. Operant conditioning typically involves the somatic nervous system, which coordinates voluntary movement of skeletal muscles.
items.why: This cross-topic link to the nervous system is explicitly noted in the study design lesson links and appears in multi-part questions combining content from different areas of the course.
items.example: Salivation (classical conditioning, Pavlov's dogs) is controlled by the autonomic nervous system. Pressing a lever to receive food (operant conditioning, Skinner box) is a voluntary movement controlled by the somatic nervous system.

items.title: I can identify that operant conditioning requires a consequence while classical conditioning does not
items.what: A defining feature of operant conditioning is that a consequence (reinforcement or punishment) must follow the behaviour for learning to occur. Classical conditioning does not involve any consequence; instead, learning occurs through the repeated pairing of two stimuli.
items.why: Students sometimes incorrectly apply consequence-based reasoning to classical conditioning scenarios, so being clear that consequences are absent from classical conditioning prevents this error.
items.example: Dudley the dog wagging his tail at the sound of a jacket being removed did not require any reward or punishment; the association between the sound (NS) and the walk (UCS) was sufficient. No consequence was delivered to Dudley for his tail-wagging behaviour.
